The local AI budget post was about how to get value out of your local GPU. This one is about seeing more from your data â how millfolio renders model-generated analytics without ever letting a model touch markup, styles, or the DOM. The feature is called Millwright , and itâs built as three nested layers, each one a plain data contract the client validates before rendering.

## Layer 1: the widget â typed results, not markup

A widgetâs content is the output of a small program â the same sandboxed programs that answer one-off questions in Ask. A program never returns HTML or markdown. It returns a result spec : a versioned JSON envelope of typed blocks â

{ "v" : 1 , "text" : "Your top 5 merchants over the last 3 months." , "data" : [{ "kind" : "table" , "headers" : [ "Merchant" , "Spent" ], "rows" : [[{ "type" : "text" , "value" : "WHOLE FOODS" }, { "type" : "money" , "raw" : 612.4 , "text" : "$612.40" }]] }] }

Every value is typed â money crosses the boundary as {raw, text} so the chart axis uses the number and the label uses the exact formatted string; the client never parses "$612.40" back out of a display string. Besides tables there are KPIs, time/category series, share-of-whole pies, and an offline proportional-symbol map. The renderer picks the visualization from the dataâs shape; the program only says what the data is .

This is the trusted-chrome invariant: programs produce data, the chrome manages interactions. When a table column is tagged as a merchant or tag, the chrome â not the program â turns cells into deep links into your Vault records. A generated program canât inject a link any more than it can inject a script tag, because there is nowhere in the contract to put one.

## Layer 2: the Board â a semantic, versioned spec

The Board itself is another plain document: an ordered list of widgets, each with an id, a title, a size hint, and a pointer to the program that computes it. Editing is where it gets interesting. Every change â resize a tile, edit a program, remove a widget â produces a new content-addressed version of the spec (a 16-hex FNV-1a of its bytes), appended to a version log. The âcurrentâ board is just a pointer into that log, so undo is a pointer move , and an edit that breaks something canât destroy the earlier version of the board.

Before any candidate spec is accepted â whether it came from the inline â editor or from the model â it passes a validator: widget ids must be path-safe and unique, referenced programs must exist, remote URLs are rejected outright, and structural limits are enforced. The model proposes; the validator disposes.

## Layer 3: pages â additive navigation

A group of widgets can be promoted into a page â it gets its own top-level nav button next to Ask and Vault, and dissolving the page returns its widgets to the Board. Pages are the same spec document (a pages[] section), the same versioning, the same validator â with one extra rule: navigation changes are additive-only . Generated edits can add a page; they can never rename or remove the built-in tabs. The parts of the UI you rely on to inspect what the model did are not themselves editable by the model.

## Why layers instead of letting the model write UI

The obvious alternative would be to have the model emit HTML/JSX and sandbox it. The downside of that approach is that you canât diff it, you canât validate it structurally, you canât revert it by moving a pointer, and every render is a security decision. Three data layers give the opposite trade: every model contribution is a document you can inspect, version, validate, and refuse â and the pixels are always drawn by code that shipped with the app.

The same layering is what makes the public demo safe to expose: the demo board is the identical machinery over a synthetic vault, with edits kept in your browserâs localStorage â same hashing, same validator, same chrome.

Try it: demo.millfolio.app â edit a widget with â, break it, and revert.

I wanted to use AI on my own data â spending now, health and daily notes later â without handing that data to a provider. millfolio is my attempt, and it runs entirely on any Mac.

## Donât send your data to the model â send a program to your data

The usual way to put an LLM on your files is to stuff the files into the prompt. millfolio inverts that. Instead of sending your data to the model, it sends a program to your data. When you ask a question:

- A local model has already read and indexed your files on-device â chunking them, embedding them into a local vault index. This is the only part that touches your actual data.

- A frontier model (Claude) writes a small program to answer the question â but it only ever sees an aliased schema of your vault: column names, tag names, types, shapes. Never a real value. Itâs writing code against a de-identified manifest.

- That program runs in an on-device sandbox over your real files, and the answer is assembled locally.

So the frontier model does the planning and the coding; your actual data never leaves the machine. What crosses the network is a de-identified manifest plus a query program â not your transactions.

The claim worth poking at is exactly that boundary: the model sees the schema, never the values. I think it holds, and the privacy design lays out where the line is â but itâs the thing I most want scrutiny on.

## The data stack: almost entirely Mojo

The other experiment here is the stack. millfolioâs backend and data pipeline is written in Mojo â including a from-scratch inference engine with custom-written GPU/Metal kernels. The local model reads, indexes, and answers targeted questions on-device. The engine doing the unglamorous work that makes a small model usable on a Mac mini: int4 GEMV, tensor-core attention, a persistent Metal pipeline cache, prompt-lookup speculative decode. There is some additional work to run the local model in batch mode, with different priorities, to keep your laptop responsive should you use it for unrelated work in the mean time. More will come in a future blog post.

Iâve spent years in Python and JavaScript and wanted to see how far a compiled, Python-ish, GPU-capable language gets you with far less ecosystem to pull in and audit. That trade feels newly relevant now that an AI writes most of the code anyway â a smaller surface to review might be a feature, not a cost.

## Honest caveats

- Itâs a personal project, Apple-Silicon-only, and mostly AI-written with heavy design and testing from me.

- It needs an API key for the code-writing step. The local model reads and answers, but it isnât strong enough to reliably write the query programs â thatâs the frontier modelâs job. So itâs local-first, not air-gapped. (If someone thinks a local model can write these programs well, Iâd love to be proven wrong â that removes the last remote dependency.)

- No warranty, no liability. Privacy is protected by design, but no software is perfectly secure. Use it with data youâre comfortable putting at some risk.
